content.title: From Motor City to the Moon: Shinola’s Mooncraft Monster: Apollo 11 Edition
content.text: Back to HodinkeeIn partnership withVisit ShinolaFrom Motor City to the Moon: Shinola’s Mooncraft Monster: Apollo 11 EditionIt doesn’t take a rocket scientist to understand Detroit’s profound heritage and reputation as an innovation and industrial mecca. Located in “the D” itself, watchmaker Shinola has created a new timepiece honoring the little-known role the city played in developing vehicles that rode the skyways, not the highways.When NASA astronaut Neil Armstrong planted his boot on the surface of the Moon on July 20, 1969--the culmination of the Apollo 11 mission--the world changed. Arguably the greatest technological achievement in human history, the Moon landing made good on President John F. Kennedy’s famous 1962 commitment to land Americans on the moon and bring them home again before the end of the decade.Certainly the Apollo 11 moon landing was a watershed moment for the NASA program, which ran from 1961 to 1975 and comprised 6 successful moon landings. But there were many highlights: Apollo 8’s first manned NASA flight to reach the moon and orbit and Apollo 13’s dramatic mission failure and subsequent crew rescue among them. The accelerated schedule and technical challenges were, to say the least, daunting, but that era remains as one of the most inspiring times in history. Even if you are familiar with that history, what you might not know is that Detroit, and specifically three automakers, harnessed their labor, research, fortitude and fabrication might to transcend four-wheeled manufacturing and make Apollo 11, and the Apollo space program, possible in the first place.Rocket PartsChrysler’s Aerospace Division took on the challenge to develop the Saturn I and Saturn IB rocket’s first stage power plants, the massive engines that lifted the early Apollo vehicles off the gantry at Cape Canaveral and started their journeys into space. General Motors worked with NASA on precision navigation systems and components for the Apollo program, culminating in GM’s involvement in the Lunar Rover vehicle--debuting for 1971‘s Apollo 15 mission--by creating cutting-edge lightweight wheels for navigating the lunar surface. And the fabled Mission Control facility in Houston? It might as well have had a Ford logo on the door (the automaker’s Philco-Ford subsidiary was the prime contractor for the iconic control consoles, allowing humans on the ground to keep the humans in space on target and safe). The tenacity of nearly 400,000 Americans, many of them in Detroit, made it all possible.Wrist RocketHometown watchmaker Shinola has elevated its popular Automatic Monster series of timepieces with a new limited-edition wristwatch that captures the spirit and heritage of the country’s estimable early space exploration efforts. Not only is the Shinola Mooncraft Monster: Apollo 11 Edition that maker’s very first manual-wind chronograph, its materials and design approach present an homage to the very concept of the “space age” itself.Based on the tried-and-true Sellita SW510 M b hand-wound chronograph movement, which carries a minimum power reserve of 58 hours, the accuracy of the three classically placed sub-dials (30 minutes at 3 o’clock, 12 hours at 6 o’clock, and small seconds at 9 o’clock) is a given. The movement itself is Black Ruthenium-plated with golden yellow badging, amping a fairly straightforward movement design into a more technical/instrumentation direction, all visible through the timepiece’s “cockpit window” case back.Those sub-dials are elegantly recessed on a rich blue sandblasted sunray-finish dial with red hands and gauging details and a gauged creamy white outer ring all framed by a gleaming blue aluminum uni-directional bezel: A truly American colorway, to be sure. Classic mushroom chronograph pushers, the textured edge of the bezel, and the cross-hatched crown grip further support the instrumentation vibe of the design. The signature, and in this case very apt, Shinola lightning bolt logo appears both at 12 o’clock along with “Shinola Detroit” badging and, handsomely, on the front of the crown, as well. All Stages Are GoThe containing capsule for this impressive movement and design technology? A 43mm brushed titanium case and classic three-link titanium bracelet with deployant clasp. In the watch world, we may not think of titanium as particularly vintage, but NASA’s pioneering use of the lightweight, durable alloy dates back to the early 1960s. The material also flies right alongside the heritage and commemorative angles of this timepiece, as well as the wristwatch’s box-style sapphire crystal. While the Shinola Mooncraft Monster: Apollo 11 Edition presents as a stylish titanium sports chronograph, some telling “Easter Egg” details take it into orbit. A vintage-font “Mechanical” badge over the 6 o’clock counter reminds you that this is not a Shinola quartz wristwatch, the Apollo 11 Moon landing date rides in red along the outer white ring at 1 to 2 o’clock, special packaging tells more of the intriguing tale of the Apollo-Detroit connection, and, pressed right into the case back below the serial number, it proudly reads “Built In Detroit.” This latest in the Shinola Monster lineage is rated to 10 ATM of water resistance and limited to only 500 pieces.
